subject: liston
method: For every interviewer-spoken block that mentions the subject, the next 4 blocks are collected, keeping dialogue/prose turns of >=80 chars that are NOT already attributed to the subject by the person layer, stopping when the interviewer speaks again. These are CANDIDATES: the answer to a question about the subject is usually but not always about the subject. Nothing here has been evaluated — treat as unverified until classified.

question.speaker: Brower
question.text: Talk about the – you’ve been involved in a lot of projects that feature trombones. There’s lots of recordings – you did stuff with Curtis Fuller, you did stuff with Melba Liston – that foreshadow – announce the coming of the World of Trombones. Give us the – how that idea was born, what you were thinking about in terms of the choices of the musicians that you got involved in that, and what it was like to maintain

answers.text: The people realized, from the fact that we were organizing the trombone ensembles, what the sound of the trombone was. Then more young people started to become interested in the trombone again. Although when I came back there were no trombone players in the schools, now you can find ten trombone players in a school, or 20 trombone players, and a lot of them are females, and they’re playing good. Thanks to J. J., because J. J. was the guy that really – he’s the guy that won the poll for the whole period of time that we – I mean, ’50s and the ’60s, J. J. won the poll, because he played so well.

src.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

question.speaker: Baker
question.text: Let me ask you something else, because another area that people don’t talk about, where you were taking chances before anybody else was doing that – I’m thinking now of Patti Bown. I’m thinking of Melba.

answers.speaker: Baker
answers.text: I’m thinking that you were using women in high-profile positions ten years before it became fashionable to do so.

answers.speaker: Jones
answers.text: I never even thought twice about it. Can she play? That’s all I care. Can she play? Clora Bryant I met when I was 12 years old. She was with Sweethearts of Rhythm. You know Clora? Trumpet player. 12 years old. Please. Can she play? That’s all. Whatever it is. I don’t care.

src.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

question.speaker: Brauer
question.text: There’s a date that Tad Dameron and Melba Liston were involved with.

answers.speaker: Jones
answers.text: Wow. That goes back a ways. I tell you, I couldn't begin to remember all of the dates. I did so many dates. I was just talking to a guy from Japan, a man who has got to be my number one fan. He has got 550 albums that I have made and he said that he could get all of them because they are out-of-print.

question.speaker: Brower
question.text: That isn't it is very important to Dr. Taylor, is the cultivation, or the equalization of the participation of women in this music. But, does that hearken back to may be the experience of Melba Liston and how important she was? Talk about that relationship

answers.speaker: Curtis Fuller
answers.text: Oh yeah, that was a beautiful relationship. I've seen her sit on the bandstand and cry. And that organization actually had to women and it. Patty Bowen was on piano.

answers.speaker: Stitt
answers.text: Actually, we didn‘t talk about Ray Charles, and that was my thought, but it completely slipped my mind. I know you did the tribute album to him in 1993.

question.speaker: Brower
question.text: You were talking about the circumstances that led you to leave the Ferguson band and to go on to your assignment with Dizzy. We talked about that band. In that band, is that your first relationship with Melba Liston?

answers.speaker: Hampton
answers.text: Yes it was. I didn’t know that she was as heavy musically as she was. I got in that band. I learned it real fast. Musically, she was heavy.

src.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

question.speaker: Baker
question.text: It opened the door for Diva and so many of these other things. When I talk to Ellen Seeling and those people, they tell me, the first time they saw it was when they saw the Quincy Jones band and they saw Melba writing – what is it? Reverie. That she had done the arrangement on.

answers.speaker: Baker
answers.text: And all of a sudden they said, look, we don’t have to have an all-girl band unless we want to. We can play in any band.

src.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

question.speaker: Brower
question.text: With Melba, was it a learning situation with you and her?

answers.speaker: Curtis Fuller
answers.text: Oh, I loved every moment of it because when I first met her I didn't know Gerald Wilson was her husband. Did you?

answers.speaker: JW
